Germany.0: Early humans left traces here long before history: the Mauer jaw of Homo heidelbergensis is about 600,000 years old, and Neanderthals are named after a valley near Düsseldorf. Modern humans carved ivory figurines in the Swabian caves c. 40,000 years ago, and Linear Pottery farmers brought agriculture c. 5500 BC.
Germany.1: Farming villages covered the fertile loess lands, building timber longhouses and earthworks. From c. 2800 BC the Corded Ware culture spread, linked to newcomers from the steppe who brought new herding ways and probably Indo-European speech. Bell Beaker groups followed, and the first bronze working appeared in central Germany with the Únětice culture c. 2200 BC.
Germany.2: This was a Bronze Age world of chiefs, metal traders and warriors. The Nebra sky disc, the oldest known image of the cosmos, was buried c. 1600 BC, and a large battle was fought in the Tollense valley c. 1250 BC. From c. 1300 BC the Urnfield culture spread its custom of cremating the dead.
Germany.3: Iron working spread into southern Germany with the Hallstatt culture from c. 800 BC, creating a wealthier elite of chieftains. In the north the Nordic Bronze Age gave way to the Jastorf culture c. 600 BC, usually seen as the cradle of the early Germanic peoples. Most people lived in small farming hamlets.
Germany.4: Celtic-speaking Hallstatt princes ruled hillforts such as the Heuneburg on the upper Danube, which even had Greek-style mudbrick walls. They traded with the Greek colony of Massalia for wine and luxury goods, and the Hochdorf chieftain was buried c. 530 BC with gold and a giant bronze cauldron. Germanic farmers lived further north.
Germany.5: The Hallstatt princely centers collapsed, and a new Celtic style called La Tène emerged in the Rhine and Moselle region c. 450 BC. Celtic society became more warlike and mobile, with groups soon raiding southward. In the north Germanic-speaking communities of the Jastorf culture kept a simpler farming and cattle-raising life.
Germany.6: Celtic peoples using La Tène art and iron weapons dominated the south and west, while many of their warriors migrated toward Italy and the Balkans. In the north Germanic groups grew in number. The Greek explorer Pytheas sailed the North Sea c. 325 BC and gave some of the first written reports of these lands.
Germany.7: The south remained Celtic, with growing trade, coinage and craft production, while Germanic tribes occupied the northern plains and coasts. Some Germanic groups, such as the Bastarnae, began to migrate southeast toward the Black Sea c. 200 BC. No states existed yet; people were organized into tribes led by chiefs and warrior bands.
Germany.8: Celtic towns called oppida, such as Manching in Bavaria, became busy centers of trade and minting. Around 120 BC the Germanic Cimbri and Teutones left the north and wandered across Europe until Rome destroyed them in 102 to 101 BC. It was Rome's first big encounter with Germanic peoples.
Germany.9: Germanic tribes pushed south and west, and Celtic oppida declined. Julius Caesar defeated the Germanic leader Ariovistus in 58 BC, made the Rhine a frontier and twice bridged it. From 12 BC Augustus sent his stepson Drusus to conquer the lands up to the Elbe, and Roman forts appeared on the Rhine.
Germany.10: In AD 9 Arminius of the Cherusci destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and Rome gave up conquering the lands beyond the Rhine. The river became a fortified border lined with towns such as Cologne, Mainz and Trier. Tacitus wrote his Germania in AD 98 describing the free tribes beyond.
Germany.11: Roman Germania Superior and Germania Inferior prospered along the Rhine, protected by the Limes, a wall and fort line between Rhine and Danube. Roman roads, villas, wine growing and baths spread. Beyond the border Germanic tribes traded with Rome, and the Marcomannic Wars of 166 to 180 showed that pressure on the frontier was growing.
Germany.12: New tribal confederations formed: the Alamanni appear in 213 and the Franks soon after. During Rome's third-century crisis they broke through the Limes, and c. 260 Rome abandoned the lands between Rhine and Danube. Trier briefly served as capital of the breakaway Gallic Empire, and Roman life near the frontier became insecure.
Germany.13: Trier became an imperial residence, where Constantine built a great basilica, and Christianity spread in the Roman Rhineland. Emperor Julian crushed the Alamanni at Strasbourg in 357, while Franks settled inside the empire as allies. From c. 375 the arrival of the Huns in eastern Europe set many peoples moving.
Germany.14: On the last day of 406 Vandals and others crossed the frozen Rhine, and Roman rule in the region collapsed. Burgundians settled at Worms until destroyed in 436, the event behind the Nibelungen legend. The Franks expanded, and their king Clovis defeated the Alamanni and accepted Catholic Christianity c. 496.
Germany.15: The Merovingian Frankish kings became overlords of most of southern and western Germany, conquering Thuringia in 531 and placing Alamannia and the new Bavarian duchy under their dukes. The Saxons in the north stayed pagan and independent. Slavic peoples moved west into the lands up to the Elbe left empty by migrating Germans.
Germany.16: Frankish royal power weakened and real authority passed to regional dukes and the mayors of the palace. Irish and Frankish missionaries such as Columbanus and Kilian preached among Alamanni, Bavarians and Thuringians. East of the Elbe and Saale lived Slavic tribes, and the Saxons in the north remained pagan raiders.
Germany.17: The Carolingian family took the Frankish throne in 751 and worked with the church. The missionary Boniface organized bishoprics such as Mainz before his murder in 754. Charlemagne then fought the pagan Saxons from 772 to 804, forcing conversion, and deposed the duke of Bavaria in 788, uniting all the German tribes under Frankish rule.
Germany.18: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, and his court promoted learning and monasteries such as Fulda. His grandsons split the empire at Verdun in 843, giving East Francia, the core of later Germany, to Louis the German. Late in the century Viking and Magyar raids hit hard and regional dukes gained power.
Germany.19: The Carolingian line in the east died out in 911, and the dukes chose Saxon kings, first Henry the Fowler and then his son Otto I. Otto crushed the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955 and was crowned emperor in 962, founding the Holy Roman Empire. Bishops became pillars of royal government.
Germany.20: The Salian dynasty ruled the Holy Roman Empire from 1024 and built the great cathedral at Speyer. Henry IV clashed with Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops, and in 1077 he stood penitent at Canossa. Towns grew along the Rhine, though crusaders massacred Jewish communities there in 1096.
Germany.21: The Concordat of Worms settled the investiture quarrel in 1122. The Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick Barbarossa spent decades fighting in Italy and broke the power of his rival Henry the Lion in 1180. German settlers moved east into Slavic lands, and trading towns like Lübeck were founded on the Baltic.
Germany.22: Emperor Frederick II focused on Sicily and handed German princes broad powers. After his dynasty fell, the Great Interregnum of 1250 to 1273 left the empire without an accepted ruler until Rudolf of Habsburg was elected. The Teutonic Knights conquered Prussia, and the merchant towns of the Hanseatic League prospered.
Germany.23: The Black Death of 1348 to 1350 killed perhaps a third of the population and set off terrible attacks on Jews. Emperor Charles IV ruled from Prague and his Golden Bull of 1356 fixed seven electors to choose the king. The Hanseatic League reached its peak, and Heidelberg University opened in 1386.
Germany.24: The Council of Constance tried to heal the church and burned Jan Hus in 1415. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the imperial crown almost continuously. Around 1440 Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable type in Mainz, and banking families such as the Fuggers of Augsburg grew rich on trade and mining.
Germany.25: Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 launched the Reformation and split the empire between Catholic and Protestant princes. Emperor Charles V failed to stop it, the Peasants' War of 1524 to 1525 was bloodily crushed, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each prince choose his territory's religion.
Germany.26: The Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648 turned Germany into a battlefield for Europe's powers, and war, hunger and plague killed perhaps a fifth to a third of Germans. The Peace of Westphalia left the empire a loose patchwork of hundreds of states. Brandenburg-Prussia rose under the Great Elector.
Germany.27: Prussia became a kingdom in 1701, and Frederick William I built a large, disciplined army. In 1740 Frederick the Great seized rich Silesia from Austria, starting a long rivalry. Saxony's ruler also became king of Poland, Hanover's elector became king of Britain in 1714, and J.S. Bach worked in Leipzig.
Germany.28: Prussia barely survived the Seven Years' War of 1756 to 1763 and kept Silesia, becoming a great power, and later gained Polish lands in the partitions. German culture flowered with Kant, Goethe and Schiller. From 1792 Revolutionary France fought the German states and took the left bank of the Rhine.
Germany.29: Napoleon reshaped Germany: small states were absorbed into larger ones, the Confederation of the Rhine was formed, and in 1806 he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire and crushed Prussia at Jena. Germans rose against him in 1813. The Congress of Vienna created a loose German Confederation in 1815 under Austrian leadership.
Germany.30: Metternich's censorship held back liberal and nationalist hopes, but Prussia's Zollverein of 1834 created a customs union for most German states. The first railway opened in 1835 and industry began to grow. In 1848 revolutions swept the states, but the Frankfurt Parliament's plan for a united Germany failed in 1849.
Germany.31: Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck unified Germany through three short wars against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870 to 1871. The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871 under the Prussian king, excluding Austria. Coal, steel and railways turned the Ruhr into an industrial heartland.
Germany.32: The German Empire boomed as an industrial and scientific power in chemicals, steel and electricity. Bismarck fought Catholics and Socialists but also created the first state social insurance in the 1880s, and gained African and Pacific colonies. Wilhelm II took the throne in 1888, dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and began a naval buildup.
Germany.33: Wilhelmine Germany was rich, populous and ambitious, but its naval race with Britain and clumsy diplomacy, such as the 1905 Moroccan crisis, pushed Britain, France and Russia together. In German South West Africa troops carried out the genocide of the Herero and Nama from 1904. The Social Democrats became Germany's largest party.
Germany.34: Germany entered World War I in 1914 and fought for four years against Britain, France and Russia, with millions killed and civilians starving under blockade. Defeat in 1918 brought revolution and the Kaiser's abdication. The Weimar Republic was founded in 1919, and the Treaty of Versailles imposed territorial losses and reparations.
Germany.35: The Weimar Republic struggled with political violence and hyperinflation that wiped out savings in 1923, the year of Hitler's failed Munich putsch. After 1924 American loans brought a brief recovery, and Berlin became a center of modern art, film and Bauhaus design. The 1929 Wall Street crash ended the good years.
Germany.36: Mass unemployment in the Depression fed support for the Nazis, and Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and quickly built a dictatorship. Jews were stripped of rights by the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and attacked in the 1938 Kristallnacht pogrom. Germany rearmed, annexed Austria in 1938 and invaded Poland in 1939, starting World War II.
Germany.37: Nazi Germany conquered most of Europe, and carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews and millions of others. Allied bombing and invasion brought total defeat in 1945, the country was occupied and millions of Germans were expelled from the east. In 1949 it split into West Germany and communist East Germany.
Germany.38: West Germany under Konrad Adenauer enjoyed an economic miracle, joined NATO in 1955 and helped found the European Economic Community in 1957. In East Germany Soviet tanks crushed the workers' uprising of June 1953. Millions of East Germans fled west through Berlin, draining the communist state of workers.
Germany.39: East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop the flight west, dividing families for decades. West Germany prospered and invited guest workers from Turkey and southern Europe. The Auschwitz trials made Germans confront Nazi crimes, student protests erupted in 1968, and Willy Brandt became chancellor in 1969.
Germany.40: Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik eased relations with the East, and both German states joined the United Nations in 1973. Palestinian terrorists killed Israeli athletes at the 1972 Munich Olympics, and the Red Army Faction's attacks peaked in 1977. Under Helmut Schmidt West Germany weathered the oil shocks as Europe's strongest economy.
Germany.41: Helmut Kohl became West German chancellor in 1982, the Greens entered parliament and a large peace movement protested new nuclear missiles. East Germany's economy stagnated under Erich Honecker. In 1989 East Germans fled through Hungary and protested in Leipzig, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall fell.
Germany.42: Germany reunified on 3 October 1990 and later moved its capital back to Berlin. Rebuilding the former East cost huge sums and brought unemployment and resentment there. Germany helped create the European Union in 1992 and the euro in 1999, and Gerhard Schröder's government joined the 1999 Kosovo air war, Germany's first combat mission since 1945.
Germany.43: Germany adopted euro cash in 2002 and carried out tough labor market reforms that helped it recover from being called the sick man of Europe. Angela Merkel became the first female chancellor in 2005. The country hosted the 2006 World Cup and came through the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis relatively well.
Germany.44: As Europe's economic anchor, Germany under Merkel led the response to the eurozone debt crisis. After Fukushima in 2011 it decided to close its nuclear plants. In 2015 it admitted more than a million refugees, mostly from Syria, which fueled the rise of the right-wing Alternative for Germany.
Germany.45: Olaf Scholz succeeded Merkel in 2021. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended Germany's reliance on Russian gas, caused an energy price shock and led to a major increase in defense spending. Scholz's coalition collapsed in late 2024, and Friedrich Merz became chancellor in 2025 amid economic stagnation.

Central Europe.0: Ice Age mammoth hunters lived here: the Venus of Willendorf in Austria and the fired clay figurines of Dolní Věstonice in Moravia date to c. 30,000 to 25,000 years ago. Farming arrived from the Balkans through Hungary c. 6000 BC, and the Linear Pottery culture spread from there across Europe c. 5500 BC.
Central Europe.1: Copper Age farmers of the Baden culture lived in the Carpathian Basin and beyond, while Globular Amphora and then Corded Ware peoples, linked to migrants from the steppe, spread across Poland and Bohemia c. 2800 BC. Bell Beaker groups followed, and the Únětice culture of Bohemia began working bronze c. 2200 BC.
Central Europe.2: Bronze Age chiefdoms flourished. The Únětice culture traded metal, and on the Hungarian plain people lived in fortified tell villages. From c. 1600 BC the Tumulus culture buried leaders under mounds, and from c. 1300 BC the Urnfield and Lusatian cultures spread cremation burial and fortified settlements across the region.
Central Europe.3: The Lusatian culture built fortified wooden villages in Poland, such as Biskupin with its streets and over a hundred houses (c. 740s BC). Iron working spread, and the Hallstatt culture, named after a salt-mining village in Austria, gave its name to Europe's early Iron Age. Steppe horsemen influenced the Hungarian plain.
Central Europe.4: The salt mines of Hallstatt made Alpine Austria rich, and Hallstatt chieftains traded with Italy. Scythian-influenced horse peoples lived on the Great Hungarian Plain, and raids may have weakened the Lusatian settlements of Poland. In Pomerania the face-urn culture buried ashes in pots modeled with human faces.
Central Europe.5: Celtic culture in the new La Tène style spread east along the Danube, and Celtic groups began settling Bohemia, Moravia and parts of the Carpathian Basin. In Poland the Pomeranian culture and remaining Lusatian communities lived as farmers and herders. Trade along the Amber Road carried Baltic amber south to the Mediterranean.
Central Europe.6: Celtic tribes such as the Boii, who gave Bohemia its name, dominated much of the region, building farmsteads, sanctuaries and workshops. Celtic warriors spread into the Carpathian Basin and pushed toward the Balkans. In Poland local cultures mixed with newcomers, and Celtic craftsmen settled in Silesia and around Kraków.
Central Europe.7: Celtic peoples held Bohemia, Moravia, western Hungary and the Alps, where the kingdom of Noricum formed around rich iron and salt deposits. In Poland the Przeworsk culture emerged, later linked to Germanic Vandals, and the Oksywie culture lived along the Baltic coast. Coins and wheel-made pottery appeared in Celtic lands.
Central Europe.8: Celtic towns called oppida, such as Závist and Stradonice in Bohemia, became centers of craft and coinage. Noricum traded its famous iron with Rome and became a Roman ally. Germanic groups were growing stronger in Poland, while Dacians expanded from Transylvania into the eastern Carpathian Basin.
Central Europe.9: Celtic power declined: the Dacian king Burebista crushed the Boii c. 40s BC, and Germanic Marcomanni under Maroboduus took over Bohemia c. 9 to 6 BC. Rome absorbed Noricum in 15 BC and conquered Pannonia, western Hungary, by 9 BC, reaching the Danube.
Central Europe.10: The Danube became Rome's frontier, with legionary camps at Vindobona (Vienna) and Carnuntum and the provinces of Noricum and Pannonia behind it. North of the river Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom fell apart after AD 19. Germanic Goths and Vandals lived in Poland, trading amber along the Amber Road to Rome.
Central Europe.11: Roman Pannonia flourished with towns such as Aquincum (Budapest) and Carnuntum, roads, villas and baths. In 166 to 180 Marcomanni, Quadi and Sarmatians invaded across the Danube, and Marcus Aurelius spent years fighting them, dying in 180. Late in the century the Goths began moving from Poland toward the Black Sea.
Central Europe.12: Pannonia was a key military province that produced several soldier emperors, but invasions and civil wars during Rome's third-century crisis brought insecurity. Sarmatian Iazyges held the Great Hungarian Plain, while Vandals and Gepids moved into the Carpathian region. Poland's Germanic population thinned as tribes migrated south.
Central Europe.13: Roman Pannonia and Noricum still guarded the Danube, and in 308 rival emperors met at Carnuntum to settle a dispute. Emperor Valentinian I died there in 375 while campaigning against the Quadi. That same decade the Huns arrived from the east, driving the Goths into the empire and unsettling the whole region.
Central Europe.14: The Huns made the Great Hungarian Plain the center of their empire, and under Attila (434 to 453) they terrorized Rome. After his death the subject peoples revolted at Nedao in 454, leaving Gepids and Ostrogoths in control. Roman Noricum faded and its remaining population was evacuated to Italy in 488.
Central Europe.15: Lombards and Gepids fought over the Carpathian Basin until 567, when the Avars, nomads from the steppe, destroyed the Gepids and the Lombards left for Italy. The Avar Khaganate ruled from the Hungarian plain. Slavic peoples spread across Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia and Poland, settling in farming villages.
Central Europe.16: The Avar Khaganate dominated the Carpathian Basin and dragged Slavs along on raids. Around 623 the Frankish merchant Samo led Slavs in revolt, ruling a short-lived realm and defeating the Franks in 631. Slavic tribes such as the Czechs, Vistulans and Polans settled in, while Slavs in Austria formed Carantania.
Central Europe.17: The Avars still ruled the Hungarian plain, while Slavic tribes built wooden hillforts in Bohemia, Moravia and Poland. Carantania in Austria came under Bavarian overlordship and accepted Christianity. In 791 to 796 Charlemagne's armies destroyed the Avar Khaganate and seized its treasure, opening the Danube to Frankish missions.
Central Europe.18: Great Moravia, a Slavic state founded c. 833, grew to include Bohemia and Slovakia. The Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrived in 863 and created a Slavic church liturgy. Around 895 the Magyars, a Hungarian-speaking horse people, settled the Carpathian Basin and soon destroyed Great Moravia.
Central Europe.19: Magyar raids terrorized Europe until Otto I defeated them at Lechfeld in 955, after which they settled down and their rulers began accepting Christianity. Přemyslid dukes ruled Bohemia within the empire, Austria became a margraviate under the Babenbergs in 976, and Duke Mieszko I's baptism in 966 began the Polish state.
Central Europe.20: Stephen I was crowned first King of Hungary in 1000 and firmly Christianized the Magyars. Poland gained its own archbishopric at Gniezno the same year, and Bolesław I was crowned king in 1025. Both kingdoms faced pagan revolts and civil wars, while Bohemia remained a duchy within the Holy Roman Empire.
Central Europe.21: Poland split into duchies among the sons of Bolesław III after 1138, weakening it for nearly two centuries. Hungary took the crown of Croatia in 1102 and became a regional power. Austria was raised to a duchy in 1156, and Bohemia became a hereditary kingdom in 1198. German settlers and towns spread eastward.
Central Europe.22: In 1241 the Mongols devastated Poland and Hungary, winning at Legnica and Mohi, then withdrew. Rebuilding brought stone castles and more German settlers. Polish Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights in 1226, Hungary's nobles won the Golden Bull of 1222, and Rudolf of Habsburg defeated Bohemia's Ottokar II in 1278, taking Austria.
Central Europe.23: Poland was reunited in 1320 and strengthened under Casimir the Great. Charles IV made Prague an imperial capital and founded Charles University in 1348, and Hungary prospered under Angevin kings. In 1386 Poland's queen Jadwiga married Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania, uniting the two states.
Central Europe.24: Poland-Lithuania crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. In Bohemia the burning of Jan Hus sparked the Hussite Wars of 1419 to 1434. The Habsburgs took the imperial crown in 1438, and Hungary's Matthias Corvinus built a Renaissance court and even took Vienna in 1485.
Central Europe.25: The Ottomans crushed Hungary at Mohács in 1526, and the Habsburgs inherited Bohemia and the rest of Hungary, which was split three ways. The Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1529 failed. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was formed in 1569 as a vast elective monarchy run by its nobles, and Copernicus published his sun-centered theory in 1543.
Central Europe.26: The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 triggered the Thirty Years' War; the Habsburgs crushed the Czech Protestants in 1620 and enforced Catholicism. The Commonwealth was devastated by the Deluge of 1648 to 1667. Polish king John Sobieski helped beat the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683, and Austria regained Hungary by 1699.
Central Europe.27: The Habsburgs ruled Austria, Bohemia and Hungary, crushing Rákóczi's Hungarian revolt in 1711. The Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 let Maria Theresa inherit, but in 1740 Prussia seized Silesia. Poland, ruled by Saxon kings and ravaged in the Great Northern War, fell increasingly under Russian influence.
Central Europe.28: Maria Theresa and her son Joseph II modernized the Habsburg lands with schools, a stronger state and religious toleration, and Vienna became a capital of music with Haydn and Mozart. Poland adopted a reforming constitution in 1791, but Russia, Prussia and Austria partitioned it in 1772, 1793 and 1795 until it vanished from the map.
Central Europe.29: Napoleon defeated Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in Moravia in 1805 and created a Duchy of Warsaw for the Poles. Francis II declared the Austrian Empire in 1804. After Napoleon's fall, Metternich hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815, which gave most of Poland to the Russian tsar and restored conservative order.
Central Europe.30: The Poles rose against Russia in 1830 to 1831 and were crushed, sending thousands into exile, including Chopin. In 1848 revolutions broke out in Vienna, Prague and Budapest, and serfdom was abolished in the Austrian lands. Hungary's revolution under Kossuth was crushed in 1849 with Russian help.
Central Europe.31: After defeats by France and Prussia, the Habsburgs struck a compromise with Hungary in 1867, creating Austria-Hungary with two governments under one emperor, Franz Joseph. The Polish January Uprising of 1863 failed against Russia. Vienna built its grand Ringstrasse, and Budapest was formed in 1873.
Central Europe.32: Austria-Hungary industrialized, especially in Bohemia, and Vienna and Budapest grew into great cities. Yet Czechs, Poles, Slovaks and others pressed for national rights, and disputes over language grew bitter. Poles faced Germanization in Prussia and Russification under the tsar, and millions of poor peasants emigrated to America.
Central Europe.33: Vienna was a cultural powerhouse, home to Freud, Klimt and Mahler, and Austria granted all men the vote in 1907. Yet ethnic tensions deepened, Hungary pushed Magyarization, and Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia in 1908 angered Serbia and Russia. Russian Poland rose up in the revolution of 1905.
Central Europe.34: Austria-Hungary went to war in 1914 and suffered huge losses. In 1918 it dissolved: Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary became independent, and Austria became a small republic. Poland's leader Józef Piłsudski fought to set its borders, and Hungary briefly had a communist regime in 1919.
Central Europe.35: Poland defeated the Red Army near Warsaw in 1920, and Piłsudski took power in a coup in 1926. The Treaty of Trianon stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its territory, leaving a lasting grievance under Admiral Horthy. Czechoslovakia was the region's most stable democracy and industrial economy, while Austria struggled.
Central Europe.36: The Depression strengthened authoritarians, and Austria became a one-party state in 1934 before Germany annexed it in 1938. The Munich Agreement gave Hitler the Sudetenland, and he occupied the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939. In September 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union invaded and divided Poland.
Central Europe.37: Under Nazi occupation Poland lost about one in six of its people, including three million Polish Jews murdered at Auschwitz and other death camps. Warsaw rose up in 1943 and 1944 and was destroyed. The Red Army drove out the Germans, Poland's borders shifted west, and Soviet-backed communists took power by 1948.
Central Europe.38: Communist regimes copied the Soviet model, collectivizing farms and building heavy industry, with secret police silencing opponents. In 1956 Polish protests brought milder rule under Gomułka, but the Hungarian uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks and some 200,000 Hungarians fled. Austria regained independence in 1955 as a neutral state.
Central Europe.39: Hungary under János Kádár settled into a milder goulash communism with some consumer goods and market reforms. In Czechoslovakia Alexander Dubček's Prague Spring of 1968 promised socialism with a human face until Warsaw Pact troops crushed it. Poland saw student protests and an antisemitic purge in 1968.
Central Europe.40: Poland borrowed heavily from the West to raise living standards, but price rises sparked strikes in 1970 and 1976. In Czechoslovakia hard-line normalization led dissidents, including Václav Havel, to issue Charter 77. In 1978 a Polish cardinal became Pope John Paul II, and his 1979 visit home inspired millions.
Central Europe.41: The Solidarity trade union, born in Gdańsk's shipyards in 1980, grew to ten million members before martial law in 1981 drove it underground. Economic decline forced talks, and in 1989 Poland held semi-free elections, Hungary opened its border, and Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution peacefully ended communism.
Central Europe.42: The region rapidly turned to democracy and market economies, with painful shock therapy, privatization and unemployment. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia in 1993, and Austria joined the European Union in 1995. In 1999 Poland, Czechia and Hungary joined NATO.
Central Europe.43: Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary joined the European Union in 2004, opening borders and bringing investment and subsidies. Hundreds of thousands of young workers moved west, especially from Poland to Britain and Ireland. The region joined the Schengen zone in 2007, and Poland avoided recession in the 2008 crisis.
Central Europe.44: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz government in Hungary from 2010 promoted what it called illiberal democracy, and Poland's Law and Justice party from 2015 also clashed with the EU over courts and media. The 2015 migrant crisis divided the region from Western Europe. Poland's economy kept growing quickly.
Central Europe.45: After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Poland took in millions of Ukrainian refugees and became a major military power and arms buyer. Poland changed government in 2023, while Orbán's Hungary kept close ties to Moscow and quarreled with the EU. The region also coped with high inflation and energy price shocks.

Russia.0: Denisovans and Neanderthals lived in Siberia's Altai caves, and modern humans reached Kostenki on the Don over 40,000 years ago. Ice Age hunters built mammoth-bone huts and buried their dead at Sungir with thousands of beads. Later the Trypillia farmers of Ukraine built huge towns c. 4000 BC, and steppe herders began riding horses.
Russia.1: The Yamnaya herders of the Pontic-Caspian steppe roamed with ox-drawn wagons and buried leaders in kurgan mounds; their descendants spread Indo-European languages across Europe and Asia. In the northern forests Finno-Ugric hunters and fishers lived on. By c. 2100 BC the Sintashta culture of the southern Urals was building fortified towns and early chariots.
Russia.2: Bronze Age herding cultures, such as the Srubnaya in the west and the Andronovo across Kazakhstan and Siberia, spread across the steppe, raising horses, cattle and sheep and mining copper. Indo-Iranian speakers moved south toward Iran and India. Forest peoples in the north still lived mainly by hunting, fishing and some farming.
Russia.3: Mounted nomads took over the steppe: first the Cimmerians, then from the east the Scythians, whose rich kurgan burials began c. 800 BC in Tuva. Greek colonists from Miletus founded trading towns on the northern Black Sea coast from c. 650 BC. Forest peoples lived in small fortified settlements.
Russia.4: Scythian horsemen ruled the Pontic steppe as skilled archers and herders, and c. 513 BC they lured the Persian king Darius I deep into the steppe until he retreated. Greek towns such as Olbia and Panticapaeum traded grain, fish and slaves with Greece. Pastoral peoples in the Altai buried chiefs in frozen tombs.
Russia.5: The Greek historian Herodotus visited Olbia and described the Scythians, their gold work and their royal burials. Greek cities around the Kerch Strait formed the Bosporan Kingdom, ruled from 438 BC by the Spartocid dynasty and a major supplier of grain to Athens. East of the Don lived the Sauromatians, ancestors of the Sarmatians.
Russia.6: Scythian kings were buried in great kurgans such as Chertomlyk and Solokha, filled with gold made by Greek craftsmen. The old Scythian king Ateas fell fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BC. The Bosporan Kingdom grew rich on grain exports, while Sarmatian tribes began pushing west from beyond the Don.
Russia.7: The Sarmatians, Iranian-speaking nomads famous for armored cavalry and women warriors, overran the Pontic steppe. The Scythians retreated to Crimea and the lower Dnieper, where they built a new capital at Scythian Neapolis. Greek towns on the coast kept trading but faced growing pressure from the nomads.
Russia.8: Sarmatian tribes such as the Roxolani and Iazyges dominated the steppe. Around 110 BC the Bosporan Kingdom and Chersonesus turned for protection to Mithridates VI of Pontus, who made the northern Black Sea part of his realm. The forest zone was home to Baltic and Finnic peoples and probably early Slavs.
Russia.9: Mithridates VI fought three wars against Rome and died at Panticapaeum in 63 BC, after which the Bosporan Kingdom became a Roman client state. The Sarmatians controlled the steppe, with the Alans rising among them. In the forests to the north lived farming and hunting peoples who left no written records.
Russia.10: The Bosporan Kingdom in Crimea was a Roman client, minting coins and exporting grain, and Rome guarded Chersonesus. The Alans became the leading nomad power north of the Caucasus. In the forest-steppe of Ukraine and Belarus, cultures such as the Zarubintsy may have included ancestors of the Slavs.
Russia.11: Gothic peoples migrated from the Vistula southeast toward the Black Sea late in the century, entering the steppe borderlands. The Alans and Sarmatians still roamed the steppe, and the Bosporan Kingdom continued under Roman protection. Finno-Ugric peoples lived across the northern forests and the Volga region.
Russia.12: The Goths settled north of the Black Sea, where the Chernyakhiv culture mixed Goths, Sarmatians and local peoples. From the 250s Gothic fleets raided Roman Asia Minor and the Balkans from the Crimean and Black Sea ports. The Greek city of Tanais was sacked and the Bosporan Kingdom weakened.
Russia.13: A Gothic realm under the legendary king Ermanaric stretched across Ukraine. Around 370 the Huns burst out of the east, crushed the Alans and the Goths and drove many of them into the Roman Empire, setting off the age of migrations. Early Slavs lived in the forest-steppe around Kyiv.
Russia.14: The Huns ruled the steppe until Attila's empire collapsed after his death in 453. Turkic-speaking groups such as the Onogurs and Bulgars then moved in from the east. Slavic peoples, known to the Byzantines as the Antes, expanded in Ukraine, and Byzantium held on to Chersonesus in Crimea.
Russia.15: The Avars swept through the steppe c. 558 on their way to Central Europe, and the Turkic Khaganate extended its power to the Volga. The Slavs spread widely, with the Antes and Sclaveni raiding the Byzantine Empire. Farming Slavs began moving north and east into the forests among Baltic and Finnic peoples.
Russia.16: Khan Kubrat founded Old Great Bulgaria on the steppe c. 632, but after his death the Khazars broke it up c. 660s. Some Bulgars moved to the Danube and founded Bulgaria in 681, others to the middle Volga. East Slavic tribes such as the Polians, Drevlians and Krivichs spread through the forests.
Russia.17: The Khazar Khaganate dominated the Volga and Don, collecting tribute from Slavic tribes and growing rich on trade; its elite later adopted Judaism. Khazars fought the Arab Caliphate in the Caucasus until c. 737. Scandinavian traders founded Staraya Ladoga c. 750 and began exploring river routes toward the Caspian.
Russia.18: Scandinavian Varangians, called Rus, controlled river trade routes carrying furs and slaves for Arab silver. According to the chronicle, Rurik ruled Novgorod from 862, and his kinsman Oleg seized Kyiv in 882, founding Kievan Rus. The Rus raided Constantinople in 860, while Khazaria and Volga Bulgaria dominated the east.
Russia.19: Kievan Rus grew powerful: Princess Olga was baptized in Constantinople, and her son Sviatoslav destroyed the Khazar Khaganate c. 965. Vladimir I adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium in 988, linking Rus to Greek culture and the Cyrillic alphabet. Volga Bulgaria had already converted to Islam in 922.
Russia.20: Kievan Rus reached its height under Yaroslav the Wise (1019 to 1054), who built Kyiv's St. Sophia Cathedral and issued the first law code. After his death his sons and grandsons divided and fought over the lands. The 1054 schism tied Rus to Orthodoxy, and the nomadic Cumans began raiding from the steppe.
Russia.21: Kievan Rus broke into rival principalities ruled by branches of Rurik's family. Moscow is first mentioned in 1147, and Vladimir-Suzdal in the northeast grew strong enough for Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky to sack Kyiv in 1169. Novgorod became a merchant republic with an elected leadership and links to the Hanse.
Russia.22: The Mongols defeated the Rus at the Kalka in 1223 and from 1237 to 1240 conquered nearly all the principalities, sacking Kyiv. The Golden Horde ruled from Sarai, demanding tribute and confirming princes. Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod beat Swedes and Teutonic Knights, while Lithuania expanded into western Rus lands.
Russia.23: Moscow rose as the Mongols' favored tax collector under Ivan I, and the head of the Russian church moved there. Lithuania took Kyiv and much of today's Ukraine and Belarus. In 1380 Dmitry Donskoy won the first major victory over the Mongols at Kulikovo, though the Horde burned Moscow in 1382.
Russia.24: The Golden Horde broke apart into rival khanates. Ivan III (1462 to 1505) gathered the Russian lands, annexed Novgorod in 1478 and ended Mongol overlordship in 1480. He married a Byzantine princess, rebuilt the Moscow Kremlin with Italian architects and presented Moscow as heir to fallen Constantinople.
Russia.25: Ivan IV was crowned the first tsar in 1547 and conquered Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, gaining the whole Volga. His later reign turned to terror with the oprichnina and a long, failed Livonian War. Cossacks led by Yermak began the conquest of Siberia, while peasants were increasingly tied to the land.
Russia.26: The Time of Troubles brought famine, pretenders and Polish occupation of Moscow until the Romanovs took the throne in 1613. Russians reached the Pacific in 1639, serfdom became law in 1649, and Ukrainian Cossacks under Khmelnytsky joined the tsar in 1654. A church schism created the Old Believers.
Russia.27: Peter the Great modernized the army and state on Western lines, defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and founded St. Petersburg in 1703 as his window on Europe. In 1721 he proclaimed the Russian Empire. After his death in 1725 a series of palace coups put empresses such as Anna and Elizabeth on the throne.
Russia.28: Catherine the Great (1762 to 1796) expanded the empire to the Black Sea, annexing Crimea in 1783, and took huge lands in the partitions of Poland. She admired the Enlightenment but strengthened noble power over serfs, and Pugachev's great peasant revolt of 1773 to 1775 was crushed. Russian traders settled in Alaska.
Russia.29: Alexander I fought Napoleon, who invaded in 1812 and took Moscow before cold and hunger destroyed his army. Russian troops entered Paris in 1814, and Russia gained Finland, Bessarabia and most of Poland. Russia emerged as Europe's mightiest land power and a guardian of conservative order.
Russia.30: The Decembrist revolt of liberal officers in 1825 was crushed, and Nicholas I ruled as a strict autocrat with a secret police. Russia crushed the Polish uprising of 1830 to 1831 and Hungary's revolution in 1849. Pushkin and Gogol founded modern Russian literature, and war dragged on in the Caucasus.
Russia.31: Defeat in the Crimean War exposed Russia's backwardness, prompting Alexander II's Great Reforms: the serfs were freed in 1861 and local government, courts and the army were reorganized. Russia sold Alaska to the United States in 1867 but expanded into Central Asia and the Far East. Tolstoy and Dostoevsky wrote their great novels.
Russia.32: Russia fought the Ottomans in 1877 to 1878 to support Balkan Slavs. Revolutionaries assassinated Alexander II in 1881, and Alexander III answered with repression, Russification and anti-Jewish pogroms. Industrialization took off with the Trans-Siberian Railway begun in 1891, and Nicholas II became tsar in 1894.
Russia.33: Russia's defeat by Japan in 1904 to 1905 and the Bloody Sunday massacre in St. Petersburg sparked the 1905 Revolution. Nicholas II conceded an elected parliament, the Duma, but kept most power. Prime Minister Stolypin pushed land reforms while hanging revolutionaries, and industry and cities grew quickly.
Russia.34: World War I brought massive defeats and shortages, and in February 1917 the tsar was overthrown; in October Lenin's Bolsheviks took power. They made peace with Germany in 1918 and killed the royal family. The Civil War of 1918 to 1922 between Reds and Whites, with terror and famine, killed millions.
Russia.35: Lenin's New Economic Policy allowed some private trade after the Civil War, and the USSR was formed in 1922. After Lenin died in 1924 Stalin outmaneuvered his rivals. In 1928 he launched the first Five-Year Plan, and in 1929 forced collectivization of farms began, uprooting the peasantry.
Russia.36: Stalin's crash industrialization built steel cities and dams, but collectivization caused the famine of 1932 to 1933 that killed millions, including in the Holodomor in Ukraine. The Great Purge of 1936 to 1938 executed some 700,000 people and filled the Gulag camps. In 1939 Stalin signed a pact with Hitler and invaded Poland.
Russia.37: Germany invaded in 1941, besieging Leningrad and reaching Moscow, but the Red Army won at Stalingrad and drove to Berlin by 1945 at the cost of about 27 million Soviet dead. The USSR then imposed communist regimes across Eastern Europe, starting the Cold War, and tested its first atomic bomb in 1949.
Russia.38: Stalin died in 1953, and Nikita Khrushchev denounced his crimes in 1956, freeing many Gulag prisoners in a thaw. The Soviets crushed the Hungarian uprising the same year. In 1957 they launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, while new apartment blocks and farm schemes aimed to raise living standards.
Russia.39: Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war, and in 1964 Khrushchev was ousted and replaced by Leonid Brezhnev. The USSR split with communist China and crushed the Prague Spring in 1968.
Russia.40: Under Brezhnev the Soviet Union reached nuclear parity with the US and pursued detente, signing arms control treaties in 1972. Oil exports propped up an economy that was slowly stagnating, and dissidents like Solzhenitsyn and Sakharov were exiled. In 1979 the Soviets invaded Afghanistan, starting a costly war.
Russia.41: After a series of elderly leaders died, Mikhail Gorbachev took power in 1985 and launched glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). The Chernobyl nuclear disaster of 1986 exposed official secrecy. Gorbachev signed arms treaties with the US, pulled out of Afghanistan, and let Eastern Europe go in 1989.
Russia.42: A failed hardliner coup in August 1991 led to the USSR's dissolution into 15 states in December. Boris Yeltsin's Russia went through shock therapy, hyperinflation, rising oligarchs and the 1998 default, while war raged in Chechnya. In 1999 Yeltsin made Vladimir Putin prime minister, then resigned in his favor.
Russia.43: Vladimir Putin, president from 2000, centralized power and tamed the oligarchs and independent media, while an oil boom raised incomes. He fought a second war in Chechnya and handed the presidency to Dmitry Medvedev in 2008 while staying prime minister. That year Russia fought a short war with Georgia.
Russia.44: Putin returned to the presidency in 2012 after mass protests. In 2014, after Ukraine's pro-Western revolution, Russia annexed Crimea and backed a war in eastern Ukraine, leading to Western sanctions. Russia intervened militarily in Syria in 2015 to save the Assad regime.
Russia.45: Constitutional changes in 2020 let Putin potentially rule until 2036. In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, bringing heavy losses, sweeping sanctions and a wave of emigration. Repression deepened, opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in prison in 2024, and the war dragged on.

Balkans.0: Early humans lived in Greek caves such as Petralona for hundreds of thousands of years. Farming arrived from Anatolia c. 6500 BC, reaching Europe first in Greece and the Balkans, and fishing villages flourished at Lepenski Vir on the Danube. Copper Age cultures such as Vinča grew, and Varna's graves hold the world's oldest worked gold, c. 4500 BC.
Balkans.1: Bronze Age societies took shape around the Aegean. The Cycladic islanders carved elegant marble figurines, mainland Greeks built fortified centers such as Lerna, and Crete's Minoans laid the foundations of palace life. Further north, herders with steppe ancestry spread into the lower Danube region, mixing with local farming peoples.
Balkans.2: Minoan Crete built great palaces such as Knossos (c. 2000 to 1450 BC), traded across the sea and wrote in Linear A, and the volcano of Thera erupted c. 1600 BC. Mycenaean Greek warrior kings then dominated (c. 1600 to 1100 BC), possibly fighting the legendary Trojan War, before collapsing in the wider Bronze Age crisis c. 1200 BC.
Balkans.3: After the Dark Ages, Greece revived: the Olympic Games began in 776 BC, Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and Homer's epics took shape. Independent city-states (poleis) grew, sending colonists across the Mediterranean and Black Sea. To the north lived Thracian, Illyrian and Dacian tribes in an Iron Age world of chiefs.
Balkans.4: Greek city-states developed new forms of government: Solon reformed Athens' laws c. 594 BC, tyrants such as Peisistratus ruled, and Cleisthenes created Athenian democracy in 508 BC. Sparta led a powerful alliance in the Peloponnese. Persia's Darius I conquered Thrace and made Macedon a vassal c. 513 BC.
Balkans.5: The Greeks defeated Persia at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis in 480 BC, after the heroic stand at Thermopylae. Athens then enjoyed a Golden Age under Pericles, building the Parthenon and nurturing drama and philosophy. The Peloponnesian War of 431 to 404 BC ended in Sparta's victory over Athens.
Balkans.6: Sparta, then Thebes, led Greece while Plato and Aristotle taught in Athens. Philip II of Macedon built a powerful army and conquered Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son Alexander the Great (336 to 323 BC) conquered Persia, spreading Greek culture to Egypt and India, and his generals then divided his empire.
Balkans.7: Antigonid kings ruled Macedon, and Greek city-states banded into the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues. Celtic invaders swept through in 279 BC, attacking Delphi and founding a kingdom in Thrace. Rome entered the region through wars against Illyrian pirates in 229 BC and fought its first war with Macedon from 214 BC.
Balkans.8: Rome defeated Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and Pydna in 168 BC, abolishing its monarchy. In 146 BC Rome annexed Greece and Macedonia, destroying Corinth, and built the Via Egnatia across the peninsula. Greek culture strongly influenced Roman elites, while Dacians and Thracians held the lands to the north.
Balkans.9: Greece suffered as a battleground: Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BC, and Rome's civil wars were decided at Pharsalus, Philippi and Actium in 31 BC. North of the Danube, the Dacian king Burebista briefly built a large kingdom. Augustus's generals then conquered the lands up to the Danube.
Balkans.10: Under the Pax Romana, the Balkans were divided into provinces, and Rome crushed the great Illyrian revolt of AD 6 to 9 and annexed Thrace in 46. The apostle Paul preached in Thessaloniki and Corinth, founding some of Europe's first Christian communities. North of the Danube, Dacia under Decebalus challenged Rome.
Balkans.11: Emperor Trajan conquered Dacia in 101 to 106, settling colonists whose Latin became the root of Romanian. Hadrian lavished buildings on Athens, which remained a center of learning, and writers such as Plutarch flourished. Roman roads, towns and legions along the Danube brought prosperity to the region.
Balkans.12: Rome's third-century crisis hit the Balkans hard: Goths killed Emperor Decius in 251 and raiders sacked Athens in 267. Rome abandoned Dacia c. 271. Yet Balkan soldiers rose to become emperors, including Aurelian and Diocletian, who built a vast palace at Split in Dalmatia.
Balkans.13: Constantine reunified the empire in 324 and founded Constantinople, his new Christian capital, in 330. Christianity spread through the Balkans. Late in the century the Goths, fleeing the Huns, crossed the Danube and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378, and the empire was divided permanently in 395.
Balkans.14: The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire survived as the West fell. Constantinople was protected by the huge Theodosian Walls built from 413. Attila's Huns ravaged the Balkans in the 440s, and the Ostrogoths roamed the region before leaving for Italy in 488.
Balkans.15: Emperor Justinian (527 to 565) reconquered much of the West, codified Roman law and built the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537. But plague struck in 541, and Slavs, with the Avars, began raiding and then settling across the Balkans, transforming the population of the peninsula.
Balkans.16: Slavs settled most of the Balkans, and Croats and Serbs arrived in the west, while Avars and Slavs besieged Constantinople in 626. Byzantium shifted to Greek as its official language and repelled an Arab siege in 674 to 678. In 681 Bulgars under Asparukh founded the First Bulgarian Empire south of the Danube.
Balkans.17: The Byzantines repelled another Arab siege of Constantinople in 717 to 718 with Bulgar help. Iconoclast emperors banned religious images, causing bitter disputes until 787. Byzantium began reconquering Slavic-settled Greece, while the Bulgarian khans expanded north of the Danube.
Balkans.18: Bulgaria's Khan Krum killed Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros I in battle in 811. Boris I converted Bulgaria to Christianity in 864, and disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed the Cyrillic alphabet there. The Serbs also converted, and Byzantium revived under the Macedonian dynasty from 867.
Balkans.19: Bulgaria's Simeon I (893 to 927) created a golden age and fought Byzantium for supremacy. In 925 Croatia became a kingdom under Tomislav. Late in the century Byzantium attacked Bulgaria, which also suffered an invasion by the Rus prince Sviatoslav, and Tsar Samuel fought on from Macedonia.
Balkans.20: Byzantine Emperor Basil II crushed Bulgaria and annexed it in 1018, making Byzantium master of the Balkans. The 1054 schism split Christianity, leaving Croatia Catholic and Serbia and Bulgaria Orthodox. Late in the century Byzantium faced Normans, Pecheneg raiders and crusaders.
Balkans.21: Croatia entered a union with Hungary in 1102. The Komnenian emperors restored Byzantine strength but gave Venice wide trading privileges. In 1185 Bulgarians revolted and founded the Second Bulgarian Empire, and Stefan Nemanja founded the Serbian state, while Bosnia emerged under its own rulers.
Balkans.22: The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, creating a Latin Empire and giving Venice many islands and ports. Bulgaria thrived under Ivan Asen II, and Serbia became a kingdom with its own church in 1217 to 1219. The Byzantines retook Constantinople in 1261 but never fully recovered.
Balkans.23: Serbia reached its peak when Stefan Dušan was crowned emperor in 1346. The Ottomans crossed into Europe in 1354 and won at Maritsa in 1371 and Kosovo in 1389. Bulgaria fell by 1396, and the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia were founded north of the Danube.
Balkans.24: The Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and absorbed Serbia, Bosnia and Albania despite Skanderbeg's resistance. Vlad III of Wallachia and Stephen the Great of Moldavia fought back. Venice kept coastal Dalmatia and Greek islands, and Dubrovnik thrived as a trading republic.
Balkans.25: Under Suleiman the Magnificent the Ottomans took Belgrade in 1521 and Hungary in 1526, ruling the Balkans at their height. Christians kept their churches under a system of religious communities, but boys were taken for the janissary corps. The Holy League defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in 1571.
Balkans.26: The Ottomans took Crete from Venice in 1669 after a long siege. After their defeat at Vienna in 1683 Habsburg armies pushed into the Balkans, and many Serbs fled north in the Great Migration of 1690. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 gave Austria Hungary and Croatia, and Venice the Peloponnese.
Balkans.27: The Ottomans retook the Peloponnese from Venice in 1715, but the Habsburgs won Belgrade in 1718, only to lose it again in 1739. Ottoman sultans began appointing Greek Phanariot governors to rule Wallachia and Moldavia. In Montenegro prince-bishops kept a mountain realm virtually independent.
Balkans.28: Russia's wars with the Ottomans made it protector of Orthodox Christians in 1774, and a Russian-backed Greek revolt in 1770 failed. Strongmen such as Ali Pasha of Ioannina ruled almost independently. Greek merchants grew rich, the poet Rigas Feraios called for liberation, and Venice's Dalmatia went to Austria in 1797.
Balkans.29: National revolts began against Ottoman rule. The Serbs rose in 1804 under Karađorđe and again in 1815, gaining autonomy. Napoleon ruled the Dalmatian coast as his Illyrian Provinces until 1813, Russia annexed Bessarabia in 1812, and in 1821 the Greek War of Independence began.
Balkans.30: European powers destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827, and Greece became independent by 1830 under a Bavarian king, Otto. Serbia gained recognized autonomy, and Wallachia and Moldavia came under Russian protection. Revolutions in 1848 stirred Romanians and Croats.
Balkans.31: Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, forming Romania under a Hohenzollern prince from 1866. Britain gave the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864, and the last Ottoman garrisons left Serbia in 1867. A separate Bulgarian church was set up in 1870, a step toward national independence.
Balkans.32: Revolts in Bosnia and Bulgaria led to the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. The Congress of Berlin made Serbia, Montenegro and Romania independent and Bulgaria autonomous, and let Austria-Hungary occupy Bosnia. Bulgaria united with Eastern Rumelia in 1885, and Athens hosted the first modern Olympics in 1896.
Balkans.33: Rival nationalisms competed over Ottoman Macedonia, where the Ilinden Uprising of 1903 was crushed. In Serbia a 1903 coup brought in a pro-Russian dynasty. In 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Bulgaria declared full independence, while Romania's peasant revolt of 1907 was put down bloodily.
Balkans.34: The Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 drove the Ottomans almost out of Europe, and Albania became independent. In 1914 a Bosnian Serb assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, triggering World War I. Serbia suffered terribly, and in 1918 the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, was formed.
Balkans.35: Greece's invasion of Anatolia ended in disaster in 1922, followed by the 1923 exchange of over a million Greeks and Turks. Romania doubled in size after the war. Yugoslavia was torn by Serb and Croat rivalry, and after the Croat leader Radić was shot in parliament, King Alexander imposed a dictatorship in 1929.
Balkans.36: The Depression hit farmers hard, and most of the region slid into royal or military dictatorships, including Metaxas in Greece and Carol II in Romania. Yugoslav King Alexander was assassinated in 1934. Fascist Italy, already dominant in Albania, invaded it outright in 1939.
Balkans.37: Greece resisted Italy in 1940, but the Axis occupied Yugoslavia and Greece in 1941. Croatia's fascist Ustaše committed genocide, and Tito's communist Partisans led resistance. After 1944 communists took over Yugoslavia, Albania, Bulgaria and Romania, while Greece fought a civil war in which royalists beat communists by 1949.
Balkans.38: Tito's Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and developed its own form of socialism with workers' self-management, accepting Western aid. Greece joined NATO in 1952 and slowly rebuilt. Bulgaria, Romania and Albania remained strict Soviet-style dictatorships with collectivized farms.
Balkans.39: Yugoslavia co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade in 1961 and let citizens work abroad. Nicolae Ceaușescu took power in Romania in 1965, and Albania broke with Moscow to ally with China. In Greece a military junta seized power in 1967.
Balkans.40: Greece's junta collapsed in 1974 after a failed coup in Cyprus, and a referendum abolished the monarchy. In Yugoslavia Tito suppressed the Croatian Spring of 1971, but a 1974 constitution gave republics more power. Ceaușescu's cult of personality grew, and Albania isolated itself further.
Balkans.41: Tito's death in 1980 left Yugoslavia without its unifying leader, burdened by debt and nationalist tension, and Slobodan Milošević rose in Serbia from 1987. Greece joined the European Community in 1981. In 1989 communist rule ended in Bulgaria, and Romania's revolution toppled and executed Ceaușescu.
Balkans.42: Yugoslavia broke apart in brutal wars: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, and the Bosnian war of 1992 to 1995 included the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide. NATO bombing ended the Kosovo war in 1999. Albania, Bulgaria and Romania struggled through hard transitions.
Balkans.43: Milošević fell in 2000 and was put on trial in The Hague. Athens hosted the 2004 Olympics, Slovenia joined the EU in 2004, and Bulgaria and Romania in 2007. Montenegro became independent in 2006, Kosovo declared independence in 2008, and Greece's debt crisis began in 2009.
Balkans.44: Greece endured bailouts, austerity and deep recession, losing about a quarter of its economy. Croatia joined the EU in 2013, and in 2015 hundreds of thousands of refugees crossed the region on the Balkan route. North Macedonia settled its name dispute with Greece in 2018, opening the way to NATO.
Balkans.45: Croatia adopted the euro and joined Schengen in 2023, and Bulgaria and Romania joined Schengen fully in 2025. The Western Balkan states pressed on with slow EU membership talks. In Serbia a deadly station canopy collapse in Novi Sad in late 2024 sparked mass protests against corruption.
